results.title: AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks Price Hike: Up 20% in 2026
highlights:
AWS raised the hourly rates of EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML by roughly 20% in July 2026, across six instance families (P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en and P4de), and the fourth rise of the year followed: on October 7, 2026 AWS raised the rates again, by 15% on most families, so that on eCorpIT’s page, read on November 2, 2026, P6-B300 bills at $16.146 per accelerator-hour outside GovCloud, up from $14.04 in July. The scope is Capacity Blocks, which AWS’s EC2 pricing page describes as a way to reserve GPU instances in advance for ML workloads. The July start date is reported two ways: AWS notified customers on June 26 of a July 1 start (TECHi), while eCorpIT says AWS’s own revised notice moved it to July 7. eCorpIT reports that AWS says the next update is due in January 2027.

...

According to eCorpIT, AWS made the July change on its pricing page without a blog post or customer advisory: the notice and the new rates appeared on the Capacity Blocks pricing page, and the October rise took the same route. AWS’s pricing page is therefore where a change shows up. The four steps eCorpIT lists, plus the date AWS has given for the next update:

| Date | What changed | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| January 3 | H200-linked rates up 15%: p5e.48xlarge from $34.61 to $39.80 an hour in most regions, and from $43.26 to $49.75 in US West (N. California) | eCorpIT |
| April 1 | 10% rise on US P5, P5en and P6-B200 rates | eCorpIT |
| July | About 20% on six families; effective July 1 per the June 26 notice, July 7 per AWS’s revised notice | TECHi, eCorpIT |
| October 7 | 15% on most families, about 26.5% on P5 and P5en outside the US | eCorpIT |
| January 2027 | Next update due, as AWS states it | eCorpIT |

...

## A block is 13% under H100 on-demand list, and the neoclouds moved too

Rank.ai’s November 10, 2026 snapshot lists on-demand p5.48xlarge at $55.04 an hour in us-east-1, or $6.88 per GPU-hour. A Capacity Block at the October 7 P5 rate of $5.970 per accelerator-hour is $47.76 an hour, 13% below that list price. On-demand P5 pricing was also cut earlier: as of November 13, 2026, AWS’s June 5, 2025 announcement says the P5 reduction of up to 45% applied to On-Demand pricing from June 1, 2025 and to Savings Plan purchases after June 4, 2025.

| GPU | Provider and product | Per GPU-hour | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | AWS Capacity Block (P5) | $5.970 | Rate from October 7 |
| H100 | AWS on-demand (p5.48xlarge, us-east-1) | $6.88 | Rank.ai, November 10 |
| H100 | Nebius on-demand | $4.50 | Raised October 1 |
| H200 | AWS Capacity Block (P5e) | $6.866 | Rate from October 7 |
| H200 | Nebius on-demand | $5.40 | Raised October 1 |
| B200 | AWS Capacity Block (P6-B200) | $14.208 | Rate from October 7 |
| B200 | Nebius on-demand | $8.50 | Raised October 1 |
| B300 | AWS Capacity Block (P6-B300) | $16.146 | Rate from October 7 |
| B300 | Nebius on-demand | $9.50 | Raised October 1 |

The Nebius figures come from Sesame Disk, which reports that Nebius raised on-demand GPU rates 17-21% on October 1, 2026; Nebius’s pricing page lists H100 at $4.50 and B300 at $9.50 per GPU hour. The same Sesame Disk report says CoreWeave added a 10% increase after a 25% rise in July, putting its pricing up roughly 37.5% since July. The neoclouds have been raising rates too. For Azure and Google Cloud H100 pricing, see our AWS, Azure and Google Cloud GPU pricing comparison, and for the H200 class on AMD’s side our AMD MI350P and Nvidia H200 comparison.

## Booking before January: an H100 block beats on-demand list only above 87% utilisation

Convergedigest reports that customers pay the prevailing rate when the reservation is purchased, even if the reserved capacity starts after a future price change. AWS’s billing documentation agrees on the mechanics: a search across a range of dates returns the lowest-priced offering available, and once you have reserved a block its price does not change. With blocks bookable up to 8 weeks ahead, a block bought before the January 2027 update can start weeks later at the old rate. AWS gives only “January 2027” for that update, and the first 2026 rise landed on January 3, so do not assume you have the whole month. VentureBeat’s advice is to check Capacity Block rates before buying, since AWS has raised them four times in 2026.

Locking a rate is worth it only if you fill the block, because the whole block is charged up front. A block costs the same whether the GPUs are busy or idle, while on-demand bills only the hours used. The break-even utilisation is the block’s hourly price divided by the on-demand hourly price. For H100, $47.76 divided by $55.04 is 87%, so a block beats on-demand list only if you use at least 87% of its hours. A block also reserves the capacity, so 87% is the cost line and not the whole decision. The comparison sets the block’s reservation price against the on-demand rate and leaves out the separate OS fee.

results.title: DigitalOcean raises H100, H200 and MI300X GPU Droplet prices about 30%
highlights:
# DigitalOcean raises H100, H200 and MI300X GPU Droplet prices about 30%

From August 1, 2026, an H100 GPU Droplet costs $4.41 per GPU-hour on demand instead of $3.39. The L40S and RTX Ada Droplets kept their prices.

By Saurabh Khatri · Published Oct 18, 2026

DigitalOcean raised the on-demand prices of its NVIDIA and AMD GPU Droplets on August 1, 2026. It announced the change in a blog post on July 21, 2026, and gave strong demand for advanced GPU capacity as the reason. The H100, H200 and AMD MI300X Droplets each went up about 30%.

## Old and new prices

On-demand price per GPU per hour. Each of these Droplets comes with 1 or 8 GPUs (the L40S and RTX Ada Droplets with 1).

| GPU | Until July 31 | From August 1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA HGX H200 | $3.44 | $4.47 |
| NVIDIA HGX H100 | $3.39 | $4.41 |
| AMD Instinct MI300X | $1.99 | $2.59 |
| NVIDIA L40S | $1.57 | $1.57 |
| NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada | $1.57 | $1.57 |
| NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada | $0.76 | $0.76 |

The old prices are from DigitalOcean’s pricing page as it stood on July 22, 2026, when it said “New on-demand pricing is coming on August 1, 2026.” The page now also lists the AMD Instinct MI325X on demand at $3.80 per GPU-hour.

## Reserved prices

The blog post says 12-month reserved rates changed on August 1 too. If you signed a contract that locks your rate, it stays until the term ends; a renewal moves to the new reserved rate. The page now lists these 12-month reserved prices per GPU-hour: B300 $7.94, H200 $3.40, H100 $3.26, MI350X $4.76, MI325X $2.88 and MI300X $1.91.

## Who pays more

Every GPU Droplet running on or after August 1 is billed at the new rate. The higher charges first appeared on the bill dated September 1, 2026. DigitalOcean told customers who didn’t want the new rate to destroy their GPU Droplets by August 1. Powering a GPU Droplet off doesn’t stop the charges: the FAQ says you pay until you destroy it.

## What to do

If you run an H100 Droplet around the clock, it now costs about $3,220 a month at $4.41 an hour, against about $2,380 at a 12-month reserved rate of $3.26. Compare both with what other GPU clouds charge before you commit for a year.

results.title: 刚刚，算力期货传来大消息！-股票-金融界
highlights:
8月11日，芝商所宣布，将于2026年10月5日推出两个算力（核心股）期货合约，分别为Silicon Data H100租赁指数期货与Silicon Data B200租赁指数期货，合约规模对应一个月的租赁期，均跟踪Silicon Data发布的相应型号GPU租赁价格指数，目前尚待监管机构批准。

芝商所称，算力已经成为人工智能时代的硬通货，期货市场可以把算力转变为标准化、可交易的大宗商品，为产业企业提供合规可靠的价格风险管理工具。算力期货的价格发现功能，将为AI研发企业、超大规模云厂商显示当前及远期的算力成本，为其扩张经营提供对冲价格风险的渠道。

东证衍生品研究院资深分析师吴奇翀告诉记者，上述算力期货合约通过指数化与现金结算的组合，把产品问题简化为谁承担最终GPU租赁价格变动风险，从而更接近电力、天气、运价等非传统商品的衍生品。

据期货日报记者了解，本次上市合约以英伟达H100、新一代Blackwell架构B200的GPU租赁成本为交易标的，价格锚定Silicon Data编制的小时级GPU租赁价格指数。

吴奇翀介绍，合约乘数730 GPU小时（GPU-hour）具有较为直观的月度经济含义。按平均自然月折算，365天÷12x24小时≈730小时。因此，在满负荷运行的假设下，一张合约对应的算力规模约等于单块GPU一个自然月的运行量。

 “企业可以非常直观地把未来GPU月度使用量转化为期货头寸。”吴奇翀告诉记者，假设一家AI模型公司预计某月需要1万块H100连续运行整月，则基础算力需求约为7.3百万GPU-hour。若其实际采购价格与Silicon Data H100指数高度相关，理论上套保规模约为1万张合约。不过，现实中仍需根据基差进行套保比例调整。

results.title: Four providers are competing to become the settlement benchmark for GPU compute. We catalogued, component by component, how each one actually calculates its price. New research at Kinetic Alpha.
highlights:
Four providers are competing to become the settlement benchmark for GPU compute. We catalogued, component by component, how each one actually calculates its price. New research at Kinetic Alpha.
The motivation was simple: index transparency and replicability kept surfacing as the limitation in our previous compute work. Our IOSCO assessment could only grade what's published. Our lender hedge-program design needed a validation approach that works without administrator cooperation. Every settlement analysis carried the same caveat — no calculation is public. So this piece fixes the record of what is actually knowable today, before the disclosure environment changes.
What stood out:
— Kalshi's Compute Forward Curves cover B200, H200, and A100. H100 — the flagship SKU of the entire complex — is conspicuously excluded. And because Kalshi's contracts settle to Ornn's OCPI, Ornn sits upstream of both ICE and Kalshi.
— Nobody uses utilization as a price input. All four are rental-price benchmarks, while operator cash flow and collateral values hinge on utilization — the two series can and do decouple.
— The real fault line is list-price vs. transacted-price: Silicon Data aggregates ~150k posted-rate records a day; Ornn prints only invoice-verified transactions from ~10 contributors. Each approach has a defect the other one doesn't.
— Zero published rulebooks. No IOSCO statement, no audit, no oversight committee — at any provider. One index restated its entire history by +40% in December.
This isn't an equilibrium. The CME and ICE self-certification filings expected this half are the largest transparency event this market will have seen — and now there's a fixed baseline to measure them against.
Full catalogue, sourcing detail, and the 12–36 month maturation path: https://lnkd.in/g25diPw7

results.title: So Meta just decided to become a cloud provider. | Meysam M.
highlights:
So Meta just decided to become a cloud provider.
Not next year. Not as a side project. Right now. Bloomberg reported that Meta is building "Meta Compute," an initiative to sell its excess AI computing power to outside customers. Hosted models, raw GPU capacity, the whole thing.
And the market immediately punished the company that sells Meta most of its GPUs.
CoreWeave stock dropped 12% on the news. Nebius fell too. Because Meta is not some speculative entrant. Meta spent $65 billion on capex in 2025 and is guiding $125 billion to $145 billion for 2026. That is more infrastructure spending than most countries' GDP. When a buyer that big pivots to selling, the people who built their business renting to that buyer have a problem.
Here is what makes this twisty. CoreWeave has a $21 billion contract with Meta through 2032. Take-or-pay. Meta owes them money whether they use the capacity or not. So Meta is simultaneously CoreWeave's biggest customer and, potentially, its biggest competitor.
The neocloud thesis was simple: hyperscalers could not build GPU capacity fast enough, so specialized providers would fill the gap. That worked. CoreWeave has a $99 billion backlog. Neocloud revenues hit $25 billion in 2025, up 223% year over year. Nebius charges $2.95 per H100 hour versus AWS at $6.88.
But the scarce asset is shifting. It used to be GPUs. Now it is power, land, and permits. And Meta has all three.
The neoclouds are not dead. Hyperscalers still route overflow to CoreWeave. The backlog is real. But the narrative just got a lot more complicated.
What do you think? Does Meta Compute crush the neoclouds, or does it just validate that renting GPU capacity is a real business?
#AICompute #Neoclouds #CoreWeave #Meta #GPU

highlights:
The market evidence he cites for durability is rental pricing. H100 1-year contract pricing rose from about $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to about $2.35 by March 2026. But the specific claim that “B200 capacity now runs between $5.30 and $7.05 per GPU-hour” is not something I can verify reliably, so it should be treated as illustrative rather than definitive.

...

The precedent for smaller operators already exists. SemiAnalysis has described Nvidia’s backstop program as typically six years in length, during which Nvidia stands ready to purchase compute at pre-agreed price levels that vary over the time period. In that framing, Nvidia provides a take-or-pay commitment to neoclouds, a minimum revenue guarantee on the underlying GPU capacity, and shares in a portion of the neocloud’s revenue earned above the backstop level. The new consortium formalizes and scales this mechanism with institutional balance sheets behind it.

results.title: Newer silicon is not always the smarter buy. | Spheron Network
highlights:
Newer silicon is not always the smarter buy.

$4.96/hr and $5.85/hr. Two GPUs, one generation apart, less than a dollar between them per hour. The cheaper option is last year's chip, and it might still be the right call for your workload.

Current Spheron marketplace pricing, subject to availability and may vary by region:

$4.96/hr is on-demand H200, with spot as low as $3.31/hr (33% off).

$5.85/hr is on-demand B300, the lowest bookable on-demand rate on the whole marketplace.

Here's how to choose:

Pick H200 if you run a proven Hopper-class training or inference pipeline and want the lowest cost per token today. The spot rate alone cuts a third off your bill.

Pick B300 instead if you need current-gen Blackwell Ultra silicon for newer model architectures and want the cheapest on-demand entry point on the platform.

Either way, you're not locked in. Switch GPUs or providers from one dashboard without a procurement call.
